title: Moving downtown after his father's death
summary: His father died on Adams Street, the property was sold, and his mother moved the family downtown around age twelve to eighteen; he later traveled everywhere but Canada.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: When did you move downtown? How old were you down this move?

When I moved down, I moved from Caldoun. I was around about, I must have been about 12, 18 years old. My mother moved from, well she moved from 719 Adams Street to 7605 Hanson. My father died on Adams Street. And quite a night until after he died, well his sisters and brothers wanted to part out the property that forced my grandmother to sell, you see. Well then my mother rented a house right around the corner, 7605 Hanson Street. And we stayed there and when we left, we stayed there, well I was the oldest, I was around about, between 11 and 12 anyway. And she moved down, she got a house down Cadiz and Willow. Well that's where all my sisters and brothers and me, we all was raised up there right on Cadiz and Willow. Well, by me being the oldest, my father was dead and trying to help to educate the other kids. That caused me to have to quit school young. You see, when we moved from Caldoun, I had got out of school to go to work to help my mother. Because at that time, women was making a very, very small sire. They was getting around four or five dollars a day, something like that. For children to take care of that kind of sire was pretty hard. Although the people wouldn't pay much, and you know, mothers that had plenty of children, they used to give them all the overs and things like that to bring home at night, you know. Stale bread, anything that was left from today's meal. Well that helped the families to go along, see. So I tell you, I didn't come up with no silver spoon in my mouth. I come up a hard way. My daddy died when I was a kid. And like I said, my mother had three other children to try to school. I used to have to get them off to school in the morning, fix their lunch and thing, and then get out. I used to go around and cut grass for people. Make little changes. Deliver milk in the evening. I had all kinds of little jobs. I was trying to learn to plaster and tread. My paran took me and he was giving me 25 cents a week. He used to give my mother a dollar and a half for my earning, but he'd give me 25 cents for my spending chance. And try to learn me to tread, which it did benefit me in the near future, because I did it enough to, you know, get some money out of it. But I worked on the riverfront. And I've been a Pullman porter. I came back and I worked for the IC Railroad Freight Shed. I run on steam ships after I come out the Navy. I went all down Havana, Cuba, Panama, Cristobal, Bocas, Indonesia. I went to France. Well, different parts of France. I went to Saint-Nazaire, and Bordeaux, and Marseille, and Brest. So I did quite a bit of traveling. And then the Pullman service, well, I've been practically in all the states, in the United States, except in, what do you call that place there where it's supposed to be so cool, Bob ran right there not long ago?
Yeah, you don't mean Canada, do you?
Canada. I went everywhere. You don't have to watch them. Yeah, I went to practically all of them except Canada. I never did get to go to Canada.
